blocks.text: VS Code added native support for connecting to MCP servers right inside the editor.
A tool that used to live in a separate app can now sit one keystroke away from the code you are actually writing.
That proximity changes how often a tool actually gets used day to day.
This closes out the Frameworks and SDKs module by looking at what changes when MCP lives inside your editor.
The mechanics underneath are the same MCP protocol covered throughout this course, only the host application changes.
1. Why MCP Inside an Editor Matters

blocks.alt: A developer opens a workspace, VS Code reads mcp.json, and connects to servers

blocks.text: A developer already spends most of their day inside the editor, context switching to a separate tool costs real focus.
Bringing MCP tools directly into that same window removes an entire category of copy and paste busywork.
It also means the assistant sees the same open files and code you are looking at while it uses those tools.
2. Workspace Level Configuration
Just like Claude Desktop, VS Code reads server definitions from a config file, but scoped to a workspace rather than the whole machine.
This means different projects can connect to entirely different sets of MCP servers.
A client project and an internal tools project might need completely different tool sets, and workspace scoping makes that natural.
3. The mcp.json File

blocks.alt: An mcp.json file lists the servers a workspace should connect to

blocks.text: A workspace level mcp.json lives inside the project folder, typically under a .vscode directory.
Committing this file to source control lets an entire team share the same set of tools automatically.
Anyone who pulls the latest changes gets the updated tool list without a separate setup step.
4. Local Servers vs Remote Servers
A local server runs as a child process, spawned exactly like the stdio examples covered earlier in this course.
Nothing about that spawning process is special to VS Code, it is the same stdio transport used everywhere else.
A remote server is reached over HTTP instead, using a url field rather than a command.

blocks.text: Mixing both kinds in the same mcp.json is perfectly normal, a team often needs some tools locally and some hosted centrally.
5. Enabling Agent Mode

blocks.alt: Enabling agent mode lets the editor call connected tools directly

blocks.text: MCP tools show up most usefully inside the editor's agent mode, where the assistant can take multiple actions in sequence.
Without agent mode enabled, connected tools may only be usable one call at a time rather than as part of a larger flow.
Multi step flows, like fetching a ticket then editing the related file, need agent mode to work smoothly.
6. Approving Tool Calls

blocks.alt: A tool call pauses for user approval before it actually runs

blocks.text: The editor shows a confirmation prompt the first time a tool is about to run, similar to the Tool Permissions lesson covered earlier.
You can approve a single call, or mark a tool as always allowed for the rest of the session.
This is the same approval pattern covered in the Tool Permissions lesson, just surfaced through the editor UI.

blocks.title: Review before always allowing
blocks.content: A tool that writes files or runs commands deserves a careful look before you mark it always allowed, since that removes the safety check for every future call.

blocks.text: 7. Using a Connected Tool in Chat
Once connected, asking the assistant a question naturally pulls in a matching tool if one is available.
No special syntax is needed, the assistant decides when a connected tool actually applies.
This mirrors the dynamic tool routing pattern covered earlier, just running inside your editor rather than a custom agent.
8. Combining MCP Tools With Editor Context
The assistant already sees the open file and any selected code, MCP tools add to that rather than replacing it.
A tool that reads a ticket from an issue tracker, for example, can be combined naturally with a question about the code you have open.
The two sources of information blend into one answer without any manual copying between windows.
9. Debugging a Server That Will Not Connect

items: Check the mcp.json syntax is valid JSON.
Confirm the command actually runs from a plain terminal first.
Look at the editor's output panel for the MCP extension's own logs.
Restart the editor window, some changes only take effect after a reload.
Check that agent mode is actually enabled, since some tool flows depend on it.

blocks.text: 10. User Level vs Workspace Level Servers

blocks.alt: A user level server is compared against a workspace level server

blocks.text: Some servers make sense for every project you touch, like a general web search tool.
Others only make sense for one specific repository, like a server wrapping that repository's own internal API.
VS Code supports registering servers at both levels, letting broadly useful tools follow you everywhere while project specific ones stay scoped.
Think of the user level config as your personal toolbox, and the workspace level config as the toolbox that ships with the project.
11. Team Sharing Through Source Control

blocks.alt: A workspace config committed to source control is shared across a team

blocks.text: Because mcp.json is just a file in the repository, it travels with the code the same way a linter config would.
A new team member cloning the repository gets the same tool set with no manual setup beyond installing any needed dependencies.
This turns tool onboarding into something that just happens as part of cloning the repo, not a separate step someone has to remember.
12. Secrets in a Committed Config File

blocks.alt: A secret hardcoded into a committed config file is a real risk

blocks.text: Never put an actual API key directly inside a committed mcp.json.
Referencing an environment variable instead keeps the actual secret out of source control entirely.
This mirrors the secrets management practices covered earlier in the Authentication and Security module.
13. When a Standalone Client Is Still Better
An editor integration is not the right fit for every use case, some workflows genuinely need a dedicated application.
A long running background agent, for instance, does not need an open editor window at all to keep working.
Keep the editor integration for the interactive, in the moment work it is actually good at.
14. Extensions That Add MCP Support
Some of this functionality arrives through official extensions rather than being built into the base editor.
Keeping the relevant extension updated matters, since MCP support in editors is still evolving quickly.
Check the extension changelog occasionally, new capabilities show up faster here than in most tooling.
Worked Example
A team adds a shared mcp.json wrapping their internal ticket system as an MCP server.
Every developer who pulls the repository can now ask the editor assistant to pull up a ticket by number, without leaving the editor.
What used to be a browser tab switch is now one sentence typed into chat.
Common Mistakes

items: Committing a real API key directly into mcp.json instead of referencing an environment variable.
Registering a heavy server at the user level when it only ever applies to one project.
Marking a risky tool as always allowed without reading what it actually does first.
Forgetting that a reload of the editor window is sometimes needed after editing mcp.json.
Assuming agent mode is on by default when it may need to be enabled explicitly.
Registering the same server at both the user and workspace level and getting confused about which one is active.

blocks.text: Practice
Add a workspace level mcp.json to any project registering a small local MCP server you already built.
Confirm the tool shows up in editor chat, then commit the file and check that a fresh clone of the repo picks it up the same way.
Then try marking one tool always allowed and notice how the approval prompt disappears for it afterward.
Key Takeaway
VS Code brings MCP tools directly into the place developers already spend their day, removing the friction of a separate app.
The next module, Real World MCP Use Cases, walks through concrete production examples built on everything covered so far.
Everything from workspace config to secrets handling here has been variations on ideas already covered earlier in this course.
